lesson.grammar_point: must, have to, mustn't and don't have to for rules and obligation

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: an official paper which says you can do something
money that you pay as a punishment when you break a rule
an old building or statue which is important for the history of a place
the group of people who are elected to make decisions for a city
to say officially that people cannot do something
something that tells you what you can or cannot do in a place
to treat a person or a place with care, because they are important
if something is allowed, it is OK to do it and nobody will stop you

items.situation: A friend wants to walk in the old town in his swimsuit. Tell him the rule.
A visitor asks if she has to pay to enter the old town. Answer.
A young man wants to work as a tour guide in the old town. What does he need?
tips: He has to have a permit.

items.situation: Tell me about one thing which is banned in a place you know.
The city council wants to protect an old monument. Give one rule.
You have just explained a rule. Turn the question around.
tips: What do you think of the rule?

listenings.text: Good morning, everybody, and welcome to the old town. Before we walk through the gate, I have to tell you about a few rules, because the city is very strict now. First, you mustn't walk in the streets in your swimsuit. The beach is beautiful, but the old town is not a beach, and the police can give you a fine. Second, please don't sit on the steps of the churches or on the fountain. They are monuments, and they are more than five hundred years old. You don't have to be silent, of course, but people live here, so please respect their homes. And one more thing. Our group has a booked time, so we have to be back at this gate at twelve o'clock. If you can't find us, call me. Shall we go in?

I am on the city council, and I want to explain our new rules, because some people say that we hate tourists. That is not true. Visitors are welcome here. But last summer, on some days, there were more visitors than residents in the old town. Families moved out, and the little shops which sold bread became souvenir shops. So now big tour groups have to book a time to enter, and only two cruise ships can stop here each day. Visitors don't have to pay to walk in the old town. It is still free. We simply ask them to respect the city. A city is not a museum. People must be able to live in it.

extra_audio.text: First Elena called Ricardo with news from the city council. Then she said that visitors mustn't walk in the streets in their swimsuits. After that she explained that they have to respect the monuments. Then Ricardo asked if he had to book a time, and Elena said: No, you don't have to. In the end they talked about the rules in Sao Paulo.
